title: Start simple: needs, wants, savings
description: If full budgeting feels like homework, begin with three buckets and a rough idea of what belongs in each.

body.heading: Three buckets are enough
paragraphs: Every expense fits somewhere. Needs are the bills that keep life running: housing, utilities, basic food, transport to work, minimum payments. Wants are everything that makes life nicer but could pause for a month. Savings are money sent to your future: an emergency pot, a goal, extra debt payments.
You do not need software or seventeen categories. A banking app, a notebook, or three pots in a savings account can all hold the system.

body.heading: Sort last month in ten minutes
paragraphs: Take last month's spending and sort each item into the three buckets. Do not aim for perfection; a few judgement calls are fine. The point is the totals, and what they tell you about the shape of your spending.
Many people find the wants bucket is not the problem they expected — or that savings survive on leftovers, whatever remains at month's end, which is usually nothing.

body.heading: Feed savings first, even a little
paragraphs: The single most useful change is the ordering: move something into savings on payday, even $10, before the month spends it for you. Buckets plus payday-first saving is a complete, working budget for most people.

If even the three buckets feel like too much some months, shrink the system rather than abandoning it: one bucket checked, one transfer made. A small system kept alive through a hard season will still be there when life gets easier.

takeaway: Needs, wants, savings — three buckets, sorted monthly, with savings fed on payday, is a real budget. Fancy is optional.
